## Why this work began

Co-benefit appraisals often report aggregate gains while leaving the causal, geographical, delivery and valuation assumptions behind those estimates difficult to inspect. This can make locally contingent scenarios appear more certain or transferable than they are.

## What we are trying to understand

How can place-based climate scenarios represent benefits, burdens, costs and distribution without obscuring the assumptions that connect an intervention to those consequences?

- How can local climate scenarios represent co-benefits and co-costs without obscuring causal assumptions?
- How should evidence, geography and valuation choices be governed and traced?

## How we are approaching it

The programme develops a conditional model that keeps baseline evidence, scenario actions, causal pathways, endpoints, delivery assumptions and valuation choices distinct and traceable.

The work could clarify which local evidence and modelling choices materially alter an appraisal, allowing scenario users to distinguish conditional consequences from forecasts or universal claims.

## Where the work stands

Current lab programme; the model remains in development and provisional findings are not presented as public conclusions.

**What not to infer.** Scenarios are conditional appraisals, not forecasts, predictions or universal transferability claims.
